He uses it as an example of an early analogue computer. It shows that the earliest computers weren't digital Turing machines but "analogue devices operating in continuous time" [spya-zg9me8]. input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth thinks the thought experiment fails, because its starting premise can't be met. The experiment asks us to imagine swapping brain parts one by one for silicon parts that work in exactly the same way, and to conclude that consciousness doesn't depend on the material [spya-ahtr6e]. He says the argument "fails at its first hurdle", since no part of the brain can be replaced by a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. He also notes that Hinton used it to claim conscious AI already exists [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before. Brains are tightly integrated across scales, so you can't assume a single neuron can be swapped for a silicon one while keeping its input-output behaviour perfectly intact [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is the finding that some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste. Replacing them would mean building a silicon metabolism too, which silicon isn't suited for [spya-un9fjn].

In the argument as a whole, this belongs to his first point, that brains aren't computers. It supports his claim that you can't separate what a brain does from what it is [spya-zw2m7u].

My inference is that he is attacking the premise, not the logic. The article doesn't say the reasoning would be invalid if perfect replacement were possible. It also doesn't discuss how Chalmers or others respond, for instance by loosening "perfect" to "close enough". Those replies are outside this piece.

input.said: What does he say McCulloch and Pitts showed?

cases.reply:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed in a landmark paper that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. He adds that later work, by Stephen Kleene among others, found that such networks, once given a tape-like memory as in the Turing machine, are "Turing complete." That means they could in principle implement any algorithm [spya-va8qxr].

Seth uses this result to set up his first argument. The two results together let us ignore the messy neurobiological reality of real brains and treat them as networks of simple summing units, while still getting everything Turing computation offers [spya-v5vz2t]. He calls this a "mathematical marriage of convenience," and says today's artificial neural networks are its descendants [spya-v5vz2t spya-va72zk]. He then argues that real brains don't separate cleanly into "mindware" and "wetware," so the marriage starts to fall apart [spya-b0086e spya-p4vmm0].

The figure caption describes how the modern version of a McCulloch-Pitts neuron differs from the original. The original gave an output of 1 or 0 depending on a fixed threshold. Today's version passes the sum through a smooth activation function, which makes the networks easier to train [spya-qknqjx].
